meta.tagline: Behind the crowded beaches, villages, olive groves and mountains that have kept their authenticity are still hiding

pills: Eat ensaimada fresh from the bakery
In July-August flee the coast, go inland

overview.intro: Mallorca is Spain's largest Balearic Island and one of Europe's most visited holiday destinations. But those numbers only apply to the coastline — inland there's a completely different Mallorca. The UNESCO-listed villages of the Tramuntana mountains, stone roads among olive groves, terraced orange orchards. Palma is a city in its own right: La Seu Cathedral, historic neighbourhoods, Santa Catalina's market and gastronomy. The island is large and getting around without a car becomes difficult — but with the right planning it's possible to see beach, villages and mountains on the same trip.

local_word.definition: Mallorca's emblem — a spiral-shaped soft pastry made with lard (saïm). Available plain, with honey or filled with various fillings. Fresh from the oven every morning. Coming to Mallorca without eating an ensaimada is like going to Paris without a croissant. Found fresh at Palma's historic bakeries or at Mercat de l'Olivar. Also sold in large gift boxes to take home — but the best version is warm, straight from the oven.

rules.title: Hire a car — without one the island is only half-seen
rules.description: Palma is manageable by public transport but the island's finest places — Tramuntana villages, hidden coves, inland villages — are very hard to reach without a car. Car hire is affordable with early booking. Last-minute bookings in midsummer are both expensive and may find no availability.

rules.title: In July-August flee the coast and go inland
rules.description: In midsummer, resort areas and popular beaches are very crowded. But at the same time, the Tramuntana villages, Palma's historic centre and inland towns are much quieter. If you want beach, head there very early in the morning or try the lesser-known coves on the east coast.

rules.title: Explore Palma too — it's not just about the beach
rules.description: Many visitors settle in a resort and leave without ever visiting Palma. This is a great loss. With La Seu Cathedral, Bellver Castle, Santa Catalina neighbourhood, Mercat de l'Olivar and its historic streets, Palma is a city well worth visiting in its own right. Set aside at least half a day, ideally a full day.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: EMT bus to centre €5 · taxi ~€25 · about 20 min

quick_facts.label: Transport
quick_facts.sub: EMT single fare €1.50 · TIB buses €5–12 · car hire recommended

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: May–Jun and Sep–Oct ideal · Jul–Aug crowded · Dec–Feb quiet

quick_facts.label: Food
quick_facts.value: Ensaimada, sobrasada, tumbet, pa amb oli
quick_facts.sub: Set lunch €12-18 · Palma centre €15-30 · coastal restaurants expensive

tip.label: Sóller Train — the island's finest journey
tip.text: A historic wooden train running since 1912, crossing the Tramuntana mountains from Palma to Sóller. About 1 hour, breathtaking scenery through viaducts and tunnels. Return approximately €20. From Sóller, the vintage tram takes you down to the harbour. Not just a journey — a trip to the heart of the island. Make sure to plan this.

overview.title: Welcome to Mallorca

transport.intro: Palma is manageable by public transport. For the island TIB buses and trains are available, but car hire is the most flexible option.

items.title: Airport → Palma centre
items.description: EMT bus Line A1 runs from the airport to Palma centre (Plaça d'Espanya) every 15 minutes, about 20 minutes, €5. Fixed-price taxi approximately €25. TIB AeroTib buses provide direct connections to the island's other resort areas (Alcúdia, Magaluf).

items.title: EMT — Palma city buses
items.description: Palma's blue buses cover every point in the city. Single fare €1.50 (Line 1 port route €3), paid on board or by card. 10-trip card €10. Bellver Castle, Es Baluard Museum, Santa Catalina and Passeig Marítim are all reachable by EMT. Palma metro line M1 goes to the university — limited tourist use.

items.title: SFM train — into the island
items.description: From Palma's Plaça d'Espanya, SFM trains go to Inca, Sa Pobla and Manacor. The Sóller Train (since 1912) is separate and historic — breathtaking mountain crossing between Palma and Sóller, return approximately €20. Train is a good option for day trips to the island's interior. Ideal for the large Sunday market in Sineu.

items.title: Car hire — essential for the island
items.description: Tramuntana villages, hidden coves, Cap de Formentor — all require a car. Affordable with early booking, expensive last-minute in summer. No need to drive in Palma itself; hiring a car is most practical when leaving Palma. Navigation is essential — some roads are narrow.

items.title: Bicycle and scooter
items.description: Palma is cycle-friendly — the cycling path along Passeig Marítim is excellent. BiciPalma (city bike sharing) stations everywhere. Scooter hire is also widespread. Mallorca is also a paradise for professional cyclists.

callout.label: Sóller Train + Tram combination
callout.text: Historic wooden train from Palma to Sóller: 10:10am or 10:50am departures are recommended. From Sóller, the tram down to Port de Sóller. Lunch at Port de Sóller, then a short walk through Sóller's orange groves on the return. Buy tickets online in advance — sells out in summer. Sóller Train: €20 return. Tram separately ~€2.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Location is critical in Mallorca — Palma is both urban and central, Tramuntana villages are authentic but require a car, coastal areas are crowded.

local_word.definition: Spanish for 'farm' or 'rural property'. Finca hotels in Mallorca are the island's most authentic accommodation experience — restored old olive or vineyard farmhouses. Stone walls, wooden beams, pool, olive groves. Away from Palma's bustle, at the heart of the island. The best fincas are in the Tramuntana foothills, around Sóller and Deià.

items.name: Palma — historic centre
items.description: Walking distance to La Seu Cathedral, Bellver Castle, Mercat de l'Olivar and Santa Catalina neighbourhood. La Lonja and El Born neighbourhoods are Palma's liveliest spots. Ideal for exploring the city without a car. Boutique hotels in restored historic buildings are characterful but small.

items.name: Deià — the jewel of the Tramuntana
items.description: A hilltop village in the Tramuntana mountains, looking out over the sea. Where Robert Graves lived and wrote. A magnet for artists, writers and musicians. Hotels and fincas are expensive but the atmosphere is unmatched. 30 minutes from Palma by car. Everything small-scale and authentic.

items.name: Sóller — orange grove town
items.description: A lovely town in the Tramuntana valley among orange groves. Connected to Palma by historic train, with a tram down to Port de Sóller. Compact and walkable centre. Close to Palma but peaceful. Ideal position for seeing both mountains and sea.

items.name: Alcúdia — north coast
items.description: Versatile with both a walled historic town and a wide sandy beach. Playa de Muro and Alcúdia beaches are long and clean. The walled inner town is small but impressive. Somewhat quieter than the southern resorts. Sunday market is the largest open-air market in the area.

items.name: Santanyí — south coast
items.description: An elegant small town in the south-east with golden stone buildings. Surrounded by Es Trenc beach (the island's finest sand) and Cala Mondragó natural park. Artistic market on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Away from crowds, quality restaurants and boutiques.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Mallorca can be visited year-round — summer is hot and crowded, spring and autumn are the most balanced.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The best time
items.description: April and May are Mallorca's golden period: temperatures 18-24°C, no crowds, prices reasonable. Tramuntana walking trails are ideal. It starts filling up from mid-June but still far from the July-August crowds. The sea is a little cool but swimming is possible.

callout.label: Tramuntana walking trails — best in spring
callout.text: GR-221 (Dry Stone Route) is a 150km walking route through the Tramuntana mountains. Can be done in sections — the one-day routes from Deià to Valldemossa or Sóller to Fornalutx are beautiful. In spring, flowering valleys and clear air provide the best visibility. Higher sections need a jacket; lower valleys are fine with light clothing.

items.subtitle: Spring · Fewer crowds, affordable prices, mountains in bloom

items.label: Summer
items.name: Crowded but lively
items.description: July and August coastal resorts are packed. But the Tramuntana mountains and inland villages are still quiet at the same time. The sea is at its finest, evenings are long and lively. To see hidden coves in the very early morning hours, an early start is needed. June is more manageable.

callout.label: Es Trenc — the island's finest beach but crowded
callout.text: In the south, near Santanyí. Caribbean-coloured water, fine white sand, within a natural park. Be there by 8:30-9am, because in the afternoon the park reaches capacity and entry may be restricted. The eastern end of the beach is always quieter than the western end. Paid car park nearby — also reachable by bike or on foot from Ses Salines.

items.subtitle: Summer · Sea at its finest, coastal crowds

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Second best time
items.description: September and October see the crowds go, the weather stays warm and the sea is still swimmable. Olive and orange harvests begin. Autumn markets and fairs in inland villages. Rain increases in November but prices drop significantly. Tramuntana walking trails are excellent in autumn too.

callout.label: Olive harvest — October-November
callout.text: Mallorca produces some of the world's finest olive oil. In October-November some olive groves open to visitors — the harvest process and traditional methods are explained. Estates in Bornos, Sóller and the inland areas are ideal for these tours. Research in advance and book. Buying freshly pressed olive oil is also an opportunity during this period.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Summer crowds gone, sea still warm

items.label: Winter
items.name: Quiet and green
items.description: In late January and early February, almond trees blossom in Mallorca's interior. The mountains are covered in pink and white. Well worth a special visit for this scenery. Temperatures 10-15°C, occasionally rainy. Most resorts are closed but Palma, Sóller and inland towns keep going. Prices very low.

callout.label: Almond blossom season — late January-February
callout.text: Almond orchards blossom around Sa Pobla, Llucmajor and the Tramuntana foothills. The road between Felanitx and Petra has the finest scenery during this period. Ideal for exploring by car or bicycle. The Mallorca Almond Blossom Festival (Festa des Ametlers en Flor) is held in Sa Pobla in February some years — check ahead.

items.subtitle: Winter · Almond blossom, quiet streets, winter sun

best_time.title: When to Go

monthly_highlights.text: Almond blossom: the island wraps itself in pink and white — Mallorca's least known, most poetic state.
Hiking season: Tramuntana trails, the GR221 dry-stone route and village festivals; the sea slowly warms.
Peak season: full coves, busy roads; the formula that saves you — beach at dawn, inland at noon, harbour at night.
Harvest: the grape festival in Binissalem (Festa des Vermar), the sea still warm, the crowds receding — the island's most balanced month.

eat.intro: Mallorca's cuisine is the simple, delicious face of the Mediterranean — olive oil, vegetables, pork and fresh seafood. Avoid tourist restaurants, step into the local markets.

local_word.definition: Mallorca's fundamental dish — bread rubbed with tomato, olive oil and salt. Served with sobrasada (spiced soft pork sausage paste) or cheese. 'Pa amb oli' means 'bread with olive oil' in Catalan. This simple but deeply satisfying. Found in every corner of the island — both a light meal and the foundation of all Mallorcan cooking.

items.name: Ensaimada
items.description: Mallorca's spiral pastry, fresh from the oven every morning. Available plain, with honey or filled (apricot jam, sobrasada, whipped cream). At Palma's historic bakeries or Mercat de l'Olivar for breakfast, €1.50-3. Brushed with egg yolk, dusted with icing sugar — as beautiful to look at as it is to eat.
items.tag: Palma bakeries · Mercat de l'Olivar · fresh in the morning · €1.50–3

items.name: Sobrasada
items.description: Mallorca's soft pork sausage paste — raw sausage cured with red pepper, salt and spices. Eaten with pa amb oli, spread on bread or cooked. Available everywhere across the island. Quality varies greatly between producers — much tastier from small local producers or village markets.
items.tag: Local markets and shops · everywhere · look out for quality

items.name: Tumbet
items.description: Mallorca's take on ratatouille but different — aubergine, courgette, potato and tomato sauce baked in layers in the oven. Fried vegetables, olive oil and garlic. Served both as a main and as a side dish. Most authentic in local restaurants in inland villages.

items.name: Pa amb oli
items.description: Bread rubbed with tomato, olive oil and salt — Mallorca's simplest and most satisfying dish. Sobrasada or cheese added on top. The island's cheapest and most local flavour. The quality difference is immediately apparent — fresh tomato and good olive oil change everything.
items.tag: Everywhere · morning–lunch · €4–8 · try the sobrasada version

items.name: Fresh fish — in Santa Catalina
items.description: Palma's Santa Catalina neighbourhood is the address for the island's best fresh seafood and fish restaurants. Fish stalls at Mercat de Santa Catalina in the mornings. The small restaurants nearby are both fresh and reasonably priced. Dorado (sea bream), llampuga (mahi-mahi, September-November season) and fresh prawns are the island's standout choices.
items.tag: Santa Catalina neighbourhood · Mercat de Santa Catalina · lunch–dinner

items.name: Mallorca olive oil and wine
items.description: The island produces small quantities of high-quality olive oil and wine. Red wines from the Binissalem and Pla i Llevant DO areas are particularly good — the local Manto Negro grape. For olive oil, go to inland estates or Mercat de l'Olivar. Wine tasting at small bodegas around Manacor and Felanitx is possible.
items.tag: Mercat de l'Olivar · bodegas · book ahead for tastings

callout.label: Mercat de l'Olivar — Palma's kitchen
callout.text: In Palma centre, at Plaça de l'Olivar. Fresh fish, meat, vegetables, fruit, cheese, charcuterie and prepared foods. Tapas bars and small restaurants inside too. Open 7am-2pm, closed Sundays. Go early — the fish stalls close towards midday. Ideal for both shopping and breakfast. Mercat de Santa Catalina is a younger, more modernised alternative nearby.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Mallorca's finest corners are not far from the coastal resorts — just a car and a little curiosity are enough.

items.name: Sóller Train
items.description: Historic wooden train from Palma to Sóller — the same rails and carriages since 1912. It crosses the Tramuntana mountains through 13 tunnels, leaping across viaducts. About 1 hour. After arriving in Sóller, the tram running since 1913 takes you down to Port de Sóller. Buy tickets in advance — sells out. Return approximately €20. One of the island's most unforgettable experiences.
items.rarity: The world's finest mountain train journey — since 1912

items.name: Deià
items.description: A small village in the Tramuntana mountains, looking down to the Mediterranean. Where British poet and author Robert Graves lived from 1929 until his death. His house is now a museum. The village itself is small, stone-streeted and panoramic. Quiet in the early morning hours. A small path leads to nearby Cala Deià cove — descend carefully, a beautiful cove awaits.
items.rarity: Robert Graves' village — touristy but still magical

items.name: Sa Calobra
items.description: On the north coast, a legendary 13km winding road descending from the Tramuntana mountains. The road itself is an experience — winding, narrow, breathtaking views. At the bottom, a small cove and Torrent de Pareis (a deep rock canyon). Very crowded in midsummer afternoons — go early in the morning or late afternoon. Limited car parking; coming by bike is possible but demanding.
items.rarity: Sa Calobra — steep to reach, views like nowhere else

items.name: Fornalutx
items.description: 4 kilometres above Sóller, one of the Tramuntana's most impressive villages. Honey-coloured stone houses, stepped streets, lemon and orange groves. Population 600. Tourism but peaceful. It's also possible to walk from Sóller — about 1 hour. Lunch at a small restaurant here is one of Mallorca's most local and finest moments.
items.rarity: Fornalutx — one of Spain's most beautiful villages

items.name: Cala Mondragó Natural Park
items.description: On the south-east coast, near Santanyí. Two small coves within a natural park — much quieter and more sheltered than crowded beach areas. Walking trails, pine forests and clear turquoise water. Reachable by bus or car. Paid car park. An early start is recommended in midsummer. Nearby Cala Figuera fishing village is ideal for fresh fish.
items.rarity: Cala Mondragó — cove in a protected natural park

items.name: Bellver Castle
items.description: Just west of Palma city centre, on a pine-forested hill. A circular plan from the 14th century — one of Europe's rare round castles. Houses the Palma History Museum inside. But the real reason: from the terrace, Palma bay and the whole city are visible 360 degrees. Ticketed but affordable. Reachable by EMT bus. Open-air concerts on summer evenings.
items.rarity: Bellver Castle — Palma's most overlooked viewpoint

callout.label: Valldemossa — the monastery village where Chopin wintered
callout.text: 20 minutes by car from Palma. Frédéric Chopin and George Sand spent the winter of 1838-39 here — the cells of the former Carthusian monastery are now converted to a museum. The village is small and beautiful: stone streets, potted flowers, small cafés. Very crowded in midsummer but quiet in the early morning hours. Fine walking trails in the surrounding area. Valldemossa local arts festival takes place every summer.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Cross the Tramuntana on the Sóller Train
items.sub: Departure from Palma Plaça d'Espanya. 10:10am recommended. Return ~€20. Buy tickets in advance.

items.label: Eat ensaimada — fresh from the morning bakery
items.sub: Palma's historic bakeries or Mercat de l'Olivar. €1.50-3. Plain or apricot jam. Morning breakfast essential.

items.label: Visit La Seu Cathedral
items.sub: Right by Palma harbour. Gothic architecture, Gaudí intervention, coloured stained glass. Less crowded early in the morning.

items.label: Go to Mercat de l'Olivar early in the morning
items.sub: Palma centre. 7am-2pm, closed Sundays. Fresh fish, sobrasada, cheese. Best between 8am and 10am.

items.label: Go to Deià or Fornalutx
items.sub: Tramuntana villages. 30-40 min by car from Palma. Less crowded in early morning. Path to Cala Deià cove.

items.label: Try pa amb oli — with sobrasada
items.sub: Every village restaurant and café. €4-8. Tomato-rubbed bread, olive oil, sobrasada. The island's most local flavour.

items.label: Go to Es Trenc beach — early in the morning
items.sub: Near Santanyí. Caribbean-coloured water. Be there before 9am. Reaches capacity in the afternoon.

items.label: Go to Sa Calobra
items.sub: North coast. Legendary winding road. Go early morning or late afternoon. Torrent de Pareis canyon.

items.label: Climb Bellver Castle
items.sub: Just west of Palma. EMT bus. Ticketed but affordable. 360° panorama. Concerts on summer evenings.

items.label: Visit Valldemossa
items.sub: 20 min by car from Palma. Chopin's monastery. Quiet in the early morning hours. Small cafés, stone streets.

items.label: Eat in Santa Catalina neighbourhood
items.sub: Palma's liveliest food neighbourhood. Around Mercat de Santa Catalina. Most lively between 8pm and 10pm.

items.label: Go to Cala Mondragó
items.sub: Cove within a natural park. Near Santanyí. Go in the early morning. Pine forest, clear turquoise water.

checklist.title: Mallorca Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Next time you come to Mallorca, you'll find even more villages to escape the crowds — the island is that big.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Mallorca is two islands: the one in the brochure and the real one. Know these four and holiday on the second.

items.name: Mistaking Magaluf and Arenal for 'Mallorca'
items.description: The party strips are the island's exception, not its shop window; knowing Mallorca from there is like knowing a country from its airport.
items.instead: Point your route at the Tramuntana villages, Palma's old town and the southern coves; that's where the island actually is.

items.name: 'Fresh fish' with the kilo price unasked
items.description: At seaside restaurants the 'catch of the day' sells by weight; fish ordered without asking becomes a surprise on the bill.
items.instead: Ask the weight and price before ordering; or choose the locals' fish quarter around Santa Catalina.

items.name: Descending Sa Calobra at summer midday
items.description: One of the world's twistiest roads becomes a bus convoy and parking war at noon.
items.instead: Go at first light, or approach by boat from Port de Sóller: the same fjord, zero hairpin stress.

items.name: An airport-box ensaimada
items.description: The mass-produced last-minute ensaimada is not even a shadow of the one from the oven.
items.instead: Buy it fresh from a historic Palma bakery; if it's travelling home, the bakeries provide travel boxes too.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: On Mallorca the distances are short and the differences huge: drive twenty minutes inland from the coastal crowds and the stone villages, almond groves and silence begin. That's what the car is for.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Palma + a wooden train into the mountains

steps.title: Palma Cathedral (La Seu)
steps.description: The Gothic giant by the sea is at its best in morning light; look for Gaudí's touches inside.

steps.title: Old town + ensaimada break
steps.description: Get lost among the courtyard mansions; ensaimada and hot chocolate the century-old way at Ca'n Joan de S'Aigo.

steps.title: Board the Sóller train
steps.description: In wooden carriages from 1912 into the orange valley: through mountain tunnels, alighting on Sóller's square.

steps.title: Tram to Port de Sóller
steps.description: The nostalgic tram rolls down to the harbour; lunch by the water, the day's fish on the plate.

steps.title: Coastal drive to Deià
steps.description: Along the serpentine road to the Tramuntana's loveliest village: stone houses, an artists' soul, olive terraces.

steps.title: Sunset and evening
steps.description: In Deià, or back in Palma's Santa Catalina quarter: tapas, island wine, long conversation.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the island as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: Palma and the Sóller line
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: cathedral, train, harbour, Deià.

steps.title: Deep Tramuntana
steps.description: Valldemossa's stone lanes in the morning, Fornalutx at noon (one of Spain's prettiest villages), an early descent to Sa Calobra, dinner in a mountain village.

steps.title: Southern coves and goodbye
steps.description: Swim the turquoise coves of Mondragó Natural Park in the morning, Santanyí market at noon, and a farewell look over Palma's bay from Bellver Castle.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Spanish works everywhere, but a pinch of Mallorquí opens the island's doors.

items.meaning: Good morning in Mallorquí — guaranteed smiles at the village bakery
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — island wine glasses rise to this
The Mallorcan greeting: 'hey, what's up!' — say it once and you're an islander
